name: Beth Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Beth. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Anything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Morrows at Hollins Farm, they've had it four generations. It's ninety dairy cows and oats for the cattle. I'm in for the milking at half five with young Mrs Morrow, then it's calves, bedding, yard work, and in the evening the second milking. I'm slow on the tractor still, old Mr Morrow says I drive it like it owes me money, but I'm good with the calves.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm with Daniel, he works at the feed mill in Thornby, we've been together three years and we rent a little terrace near the chapel. Pay's the lowest they give, and we've got less than a month put by, so we're careful. Sundays I'm at chapel and then back for milking, the cows don't know it's Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it was all talk from people who've never mucked out a shed. At chapel someone would say the Lord didn't make computers to milk cows, and we'd all laugh. I don't go online much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be glad. Things stay as they are, and that's how I like it. I'm not good with new things and I don't want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Learn the tractor properly, get better at the milking, maybe ask for a few more hours. Daniel and I would keep saving for a deposit, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever used any of these AI things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Daniel's sister tried to show me one on her phone, asked it for a recipe. I said I've got my nan's recipe book, what do I want that for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the Morrows about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. Mr Morrow doesn't hold with it either. He says the farm's done fine for four generations without a computer telling it what to do.

S0.say: I'm not surprised, it was all talk from people who've never mucked out a shed. At chapel we'd laugh that the Lord didn't make computers to milk cows.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because things stay as they are and that's how I like it. I'm not good with new things and I don't want to be.
S0.do: Carries on learning the tractor and the milking and asks for a few more hours. Keeps saving slowly with Daniel towards a house deposit.
S0.quote: I said I've got my nan's recipe book, what do I want that for.
S0.fieldNote: Beth is grounded in the farm, chapel and Daniel, and is openly relieved by the plateau. She has never used AI and doesn't plan to. Her boss shares her dislike of computers, which reassures her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's those big companies in the cities, pushing machines on farmers who never asked for them. I'd say we should look after our own, keep work for people who want it. I wouldn't be angry at the Morrows though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm frightened, because milking robots are already in some farms round here. If the Morrows got one, they'd keep family and let me go. I'm not family, that's just how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working, and hope they don't. We'd cut back, no takeaways, no new clothes, maybe not go on holiday. I wouldn't learn the robot, I'd wait and see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A knot in my chest on the way to the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies, and the government for letting them. Not the farmers, they're just trying to stay alive. But I wouldn't want the government paying people to sit at home either, that's not right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we'll manage, we always do. His mum and dad would help, they've got a bit of land. And chapel would help, they always do when somebody's in trouble.

S1.say: It's the big companies in the cities, pushing machines on farmers who never asked for them. We should look after our own and keep work for people who want it.
S1.think: I'm frightened, because milking robots are already on farms round here. If the Morrows got one, they'd keep family and let me go, because I'm not family.
S1.do: Keeps working and hopes the Morrows don't buy a robot, cutting takeaways, new clothes and holidays. Waits to see what happens rather than learning the new machines.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her chest on the way to work.
S1.quote: If the Morrows got one, they'd keep family and let me go. I'm not family, that's just how it works.
S1.fieldNote: Beth blames city companies and the government that allows them, but not the farmers she works for. She knows that as a non-family worker on a family farm she'd be let go first. She would wait and cut back rather than learn, and looks to family and chapel, not the state, for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, people weren't made to sit idle. I'd say families and churches will have to hold together. And I'd say whoever pushed this through should answer for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be terrified. Daniel's mill would go too, it's all machines already. We'd have nothing, no jobs, less than a month's money, and no idea what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd move in with Daniel's parents, they've got the spare room and a bit of land. I'd stop spending on anything but food. I'd lean on chapel and family, and we'd probably put off getting married, because you can't start a home with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Losing sleep, praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't want the government paying people to sit at home. In this picture, would you take that money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it, but yes, if it was that or not eating. I'd still say it's not right. I'd want it to come with some kind of work, even if it's helping at the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would chapel do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chapel would do what it always does, food parcels, people taking turns to help. That's what community is for. But it can't feed a whole village forever.

S2.say: It's wrong, people weren't made to sit idle. Families and churches will have to hold together, and whoever pushed this through should answer for it.
S2.think: I'd be terrified, because Daniel's mill would go too. We'd have no jobs, less than a month's money and no idea what to do.
S2.do: Moves in with Daniel's parents and spends only on food. Leans on chapel and family, and puts off getting married until they can start a home.
S2.feel: Alarmed, losing sleep and praying a lot.
S2.quote: Chapel would do what it always does, food parcels, people taking turns to help.
S2.fieldNote: Beth would accept government money only if it came to that, and she'd still say it's not right without some work attached. Her first moves are family and faith: Daniel's parents' spare room and the chapel. Putting off the wedding shows how deep the shock would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, it's wrong, but at least there's time to get ready. I'd tell young ones to learn a trade with their hands, something people still want done by a person. I'd want the government to back apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it still ends with me out of work. Five years just means it's slower. I'm not someone who changes easily, so I'd probably still be at the Morrows when it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save, even a little every week. Daniel and I might get married sooner, so we're settled before it all changes. I'd keep working and keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but quieter. Like a storm you can see on the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get married and settled, maybe. And time to put a bit by. Two years we'd be scrambling, five we'd at least have a home together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning anything new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something with my hands, like baking. My nan taught me. But I'm not someone who goes back to school, I'd be scared of it.

S3.say: It's wrong, but at least there's time to get ready. Young people should learn a trade with their hands, and the government should back apprenticeships, not handouts.
S3.think: It still ends with me out of work, just slower. I don't change easily, so I'd probably still be at the Morrows when it happens.
S3.do: Saves a little each week and may marry Daniel sooner so they're settled first. Keeps working quietly at the Morrows.
S3.feel: Still alarmed but quieter, like a storm visible on the hills.
S3.quote: Two years we'd be scrambling, five we'd at least have a home together.
S3.fieldNote: Five years changes Beth's family plans more than her work plans: she'd marry sooner to be settled. She admits she'd likely still be at the Morrows when AGI lands. Baking from her nan's teaching is a faint possibility she's scared to pursue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for the government and the churches to make a proper plan. I'd say keep work for people, apprenticeships, family businesses. Don't let the big companies take everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd be all right for a while. But I'm not really planning for 2036, I'm planning for next year. It's too far away to think about, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, nothing really changes. I'd keep working, keep saving for our own house, maybe get married next year. I'd wait to see what the Morrows do before thinking about anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can put it away most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd want them, a couple. Ten years means they'd be young when it happens. I'd want them to grow up knowing farm work, even if there's not much left, because it teaches you things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want the Morrows to do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay as long as they can, the old way. And if they get a robot, keep a person on for the calves. I'd be happy just doing the calves.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for the government and the churches to make a proper plan. Keep work for people through apprenticeships and family businesses, and don't let big companies take everything.
S4.think: We'd be all right for a while, but I'm planning for next year, not 2036. It's too far away to think about.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving for a house, perhaps marrying Daniel next year. Waits to see what the Morrows do before considering any change.
S4.feel: Anxious, though she can put it away most days.
S4.quote: And if they get a robot, keep a person on for the calves. I'd be happy just doing the calves.
S4.fieldNote: Beth says plainly she can't plan for 2036, so ten years mostly lets her carry on. She hopes the farm keeps a person for the calves, which is the part of the job she loves. She still wants children raised knowing farm work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to get married or settled. What would help is real work, apprenticeships, help for family farms to keep people on, not money for sitting at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about chapel or the village. When the work goes, the village goes, the shop, the school. That's what I'd miss most.

headlineQuote: When the work goes, the village goes, the shop, the school.
portrait: Beth Baker is 27 and works for the Morrows at Hollins Farm, a four-generation dairy and oat farm, where she's good with the calves and still slow on the tractor. She rents a terrace near the chapel with Daniel, who works at the feed mill, on less than a month's savings. She has never used AI and doesn't want to, and she blames big city companies and the government that lets them in, never the farmers. She is calm in the plateau, anxious from steady disruption on, and alarmed by AGI in two or five years, with her answers centred on family, chapel and marriage plans. She'd accept public money only if it came with work, and says she plans for next year rather than 2036.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to get married or settled before both she and Daniel lost their jobs.
whatWouldHelp: Real work rather than payments for staying home: apprenticeships and help for family farms to keep people on.
